title: The Contemplation of the True Aspect of All Phenomena
excerpt: Excerpted from the Essential Method of Contemplation (translated by the Tripitaka Dharma Master Kumarajiva of the Later Qin); annotated by Zhanran.

inline.s: Excerpted from the Essential Method of Contemplation (translated by the Tripitaka Dharma Master Kumarajiva of the Later Qin)
Annotated by Zhanran
All marks whatsoever are illusory and false; not grasping at any mark, one abides thus, unmoving.

[All dharmas] refers to the myriad things and phenomena of the entire universe. [The true aspect of all phenomena] “True aspect” means the actual condition; “the true aspect of all phenomena” is the actual condition of all dharmas. The Buddha Pitaka Sutra says:
“What is called the true aspect of all phenomena? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever.”
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like illusory appearances; within them the Tathagata, by the power of skillful means, is without any defilement or attachment.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The Bodhisattva Mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as their true aspect—without inversion, without moving, without retreating, without turning.”

[The contemplation of the true aspect of all phenomena] To observe the spiritual world and the material world according to the principle of the true aspect of all phenomena. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Practice of Contemplating the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:

“The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born entirely of deluded thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true aspect. The host of offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can melt them away.”

[The host of offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can melt them away] Contemplating the true aspect can eliminate all offenses, just as the blazing sun melts frost and dew. The Song of Enlightenment says:
“Two monks once transgressed in lust and killing; Upali’s
(Upali)
firefly-light of the precepts only bound them the more, but the great sage Vimalakirti at once dispelled their doubt
(the great sage Vimalakirti expounded the true aspect and at once dispelled their doubt; for details see
Commentary on the Song of Enlightenment
, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow.”
One who contemplates the true aspect of all phenomena should know that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, and because they arise from causes and conditions they are not self-mastering
(they cannot exist on their own)
; because they are not self-mastering, they are ultimately empty in aspect, possessing only provisional names
(All dharmas are formed by the conjunction of causes and conditions; they have no real substance, only provisional names. The Treatise on the Middle Way says:
“Whatever arises from causes and conditions, I declare to be empty; it is also called a provisional name, and is likewise the meaning of the Middle Way”
[Provisional name] A name of provisional existence. In the Commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra, the great master Kumarajiva says:
“When conditions meet there is no reality, only a borrowed, empty name.”
The Compendium of Mahayana Meanings says:
“All dharmas exist as provisional names, hence they are called provisional names.”

, and nothing real exists among them. If a dharma truly existed, one should not speak of it as nothing; that which formerly existed and now does not is called annihilation. Neither eternal nor annihilated, neither existent nor non-existent
(being originally illusory, they are not to be spoken of as eternal or annihilated, existent or non-existent)
, with the mind extinguished at the seat of consciousness
(the mind is extinguished at the seat of consciousness; the seat of consciousness is where the sense-faculties meet their objects)
, and speech utterly exhausted—this is called the profoundly pure contemplation.
Moreover, to contemplate the dharmas of lust, anger, and delusion is itself to contemplate the true aspect.
(To contemplate lust, anger, delusion, and the other evil dharmas as illusions—
ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever
. The “true aspect” is precisely ultimate emptiness, without anything whatsoever. In the Buddha Pitaka Sutra,
Chapter Two, “Recollection of the Buddha,” the Buddha says:
“What is called the true aspect of all phenomena? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever.”
In Chapter Forty of the Mahaparinirvana Sutra,
the “Kauṇḍinya” chapter, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are false and unreal.”
Why is this? These dharmas
(these dharmas)
are neither within nor without. If they were within, they should not depend on external causes and conditions to arise; if they were without, then there would be nothing for them to abide in
(if the dharmas were outside the mind, the mind should not go out to grasp and cling to them)
. If there is nowhere for them to abide, there is likewise no arising and ceasing—they are empty, without anything whatsoever
(if the mind is free of defilement and attachment, then the mind’s thoughts are likewise free of arising and ceasing—empty, without anything whatsoever)
, pure and unconditioned—this is called the contemplation of the true aspect of lust, anger, and delusion.
Moreover, all dharmas are ultimately pure
(originally there is not a single thing)

, and this is not something the Buddhas and sages can make them be. It is only because ordinary people have not attained the contemplation of wisdom that they see the various illusory dharmas as having manifold marks. One who has attained the true aspect
(one who has awakened to the true aspect)
contemplates them as images in a mirror
(contemplates all dharmas as images in a mirror)

, which only deceive the eye; in truth they neither arise nor cease. This contemplation is extremely profound and subtle. If a practitioner can with a focused mind contemplate this deep and tranquil true aspect
(if a practitioner can with a focused mind contemplate this deep and tranquil true aspect)
, without giving rise to wrong views
(without being turned by thoughts or dragged by objects)
, he can then attain the patient acceptance of the birthlessness of all dharmas.

[The patient acceptance of the birthlessness of dharmas] For short, the acceptance of birthlessness. To realize that all dharmas are illusions—that, never having arisen, they likewise have no cessation (neither arising nor ceasing)—and to abide unmoving in this principle. “Acceptance” (kṣānti) means to abide, that is, for the mind to dwell in the principle without wavering. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, fascicle fifty, says:

“The patient acceptance of the birthlessness of dharmas means, within the true aspect of all dharmas that neither arise nor cease, to believe, accept, and penetrate without hindrance and without retreat—this is called the acceptance of birthlessness.”
This method is difficult to take up
(this contemplation of the true aspect is not easy to put into practice)
, for the mind is prone to scattering; and if it does not scatter, it may instead sink and vanish
(because the mind is prone to scattering, if one draws it back so that it no longer scatters, one instead falls into drowsiness)
. One should constantly purify the mind and observe with clarity and distinctness
(therefore one should constantly purify the mind and observe clearly and distinctly, practicing again and again)
. If the mind is hard to rein in, one should rebuke it: “For countless kalpas you have ceaselessly engaged in mixed karma
(creating all manner of karma by following conditions and circumstances)

, never satisfied, chasing after worldly pleasures without realizing they are suffering. All the craving for pleasure in the world brings calamity, and according to karmic causes and conditions one is born into the five paths
(gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell beings)

, all of it the doing of the mind; who has made you so? You are like a mad elephant trampling and harming, with nothing to restrain you; who will tame you? If you are well tamed, you will leave the troubles of the world. You should know that dwelling in the womb is impure, and suffering presses and crowds in upon the body
zé
, meaning “to press”)

, like a hell. Once born into the world, the sufferings of aging, sickness, and death, grief and sorrow in ten thousand forms, leave one without freedom. If born among the heavens, one will yet fall again. The three realms have no peace—why do you cling to them with delight?” Having thus rebuked the mind in various ways, return to the original object of contemplation
(draw the mind back to contemplate the true aspect)
. When the mind’s thoughts come to rest
(the mind is settled and thoughts cease)

, the mind becomes pliant, and one sees various colored lights issuing from the body—this is called the contemplation of the true aspect of all phenomena. One who wishes to be born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life
(one who wishes to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
should thus contemplate upward the Buddha of Immeasurable Life
(that is, Amitabha Buddha)

Moreover, in contemplating the true aspect of all phenomena, one should also contemplate the world as like a dream, like an illusion, with nothing real in it; it is only through inverted and deluded dharmas that one wantonly gives rise to afflictions and suffers the retribution of various offenses. It is like a man watching little children quarrel over
(contend with one another for)

tiles, stones, earth, and wood, and then growing angry and fighting; the various worlds of the world should be seen in just this way. One should arouse great compassion, vow to deliver all beings, constantly subdue the mind, and cultivate the two acceptances—namely, the acceptance of beings and the acceptance of dharmas.

The acceptance of beings means that if beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges inflict all manner of evil upon one, the mind does not grow angry; and if they show all manner of reverence and offerings, the mind does not rejoice. Furthermore, one contemplates that beings have no beginning and no end. If there were a beginning, there would be no causes and conditions; if there are causes and conditions, then there is no beginning. And if there is no beginning, there is likewise no middle or end. Contemplating in this way, one does not fall into the two extremes of eternalism and annihilation. By means of this tranquil
(the same as “secure”)
way one contemplates all beings and gives rise to no wrong views—this is called the acceptance of beings.

[The two extremes of eternalism and annihilation] Namely the two extreme views of eternalism and annihilation. Insisting that after death one will be born again as a human being, abiding forever through life after life without cessation, is eternalism. Insisting that after death everything is utterly annihilated and no longer exists, is annihilation. Eternalism asserts existence on the basis of existence; annihilation asserts non-existence on the basis of existence. The truth is that originally there is not a single thing—birth and death are both illusory—and so both annihilation and eternalism are wrong views.
The acceptance of dharmas means that one should contemplate all dharmas as extremely deep and pure, ultimately empty in aspect
(originally there is not a single thing)
, with the mind free of hindrance, able to endure this—this is called the acceptance of dharmas. One who has newly brought forth the aspiration
(one who has newly brought forth the aspiration for bodhi)
, though he has not yet attained this acceptance of dharmas, should cultivate his mind in this way.
Moreover, while contemplating that all dharmas are ultimately empty in aspect, one should constantly arouse great compassion toward beings
(practicing compassion and emptiness together to deliver beings)
, and with all one’s roots of goodness, dedicate them entirely, vowing to be born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; then one will attain rebirth there.
